631.event_title: Cavour wins France as Piedmont's ally against Austria
631.place: Turin, Paris and Plombieres, France; northern Italy
631.event: As prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia, Count Camillo di Cavour brought his small state into the Crimean War alongside Britain and France and then secured a place at the Congress of Paris in 1856, where he raised the Italian question before the great powers. At a secret meeting at Plombieres in July 1858 he and Napoleon III agreed on a war against Austria in the following year. When Austria sent Piedmont an ultimatum in 1859, the Franco-Piedmontese alliance came into force, and the war that followed won Lombardy for Piedmont.
631.explanation: Cavour judged that Piedmont alone could not drive Austria out of Italy, so he spent years acquiring the means (a great-power ally), waiting for the right moment and choosing a method that let Austria appear the aggressor.
631.tie_back: The kural defines the excellent minister as one who masters the means, the time, the method and the difficult task itself, and Cavour's patient preparation of all four for the hard task of challenging Austria is a clear case of it.
631._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a minister weighing means, timing and method for a difficult undertaking, though the outcome in 1859 fell short of Cavour's full aims.

632.event_title: Sardar Patel brings the princely states into the Indian Union
632.event: At independence in 1947, rulers of the princely states, covering about two fifths of India's territory, were free to join India or Pakistan or to stay out of both. Vallabhbhai Patel, as deputy prime minister and minister in charge of the new States Department, worked with its secretary V. P. Menon to bring them in one by one. Over 560 princely states were brought into the Indian Union within a short span of time.
632.explanation: The work called for firmness with reluctant rulers, steady concern for the security of the people, a knowledge of law and administration, and unbroken effort over many months.
632.tie_back: The kural adds firmness, protection of the people, learning and persevering effort to the minister's qualities, and Patel's integration of the princely states displayed all of them in a single task.
632._accuracy_note: A strong fit for firmness, protection of the realm and sustained effort; 'learning' is the quality least directly shown by the event.

633.event_title: Talleyrand splits the victorious allies at the Congress of Vienna
633.event: At the Congress of Vienna the four victorious powers, Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia, negotiated the post-Napoleonic settlement, with defeated France represented by its foreign minister, Talleyrand. When Russia and Prussia pressed claims that alarmed Britain and Austria, Talleyrand proposed a secret treaty of guarantee between Britain, France and Austria. It was signed on 3 January 1815, setting three powers against Russia and Prussia and giving France a seat at the great powers' table.
633.explanation: Representing a defeated country with no allies, Talleyrand turned the disagreements of the victors to France's advantage by drawing two of them into an alliance with his own country.
633.tie_back: The kural praises the minister who can detach the enemy's allies and bring others over to his side, which is exactly what Talleyrand did to the coalition that had defeated France.
633._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the first skill named (splitting the enemy's alliance); the kural's other two skills are less directly shown.

634.event_title: The Beveridge Report sets out a plan against the five giant evils
634.event: In June 1941 William Beveridge was asked to head a committee of inquiry surveying Britain's patchwork social insurance schemes. His report, Social Insurance and Allied Services, was presented to Parliament on 24 November 1942 and proposed a comprehensive system of social insurance to attack five great evils: want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. More than 600,000 copies of the report and its summaries were sold by February 1944, and after the war Parliament passed the National Insurance Act of 1946 and established the National Health Service in 1948.
634.explanation: Beveridge's report was valued because it combined a thorough survey of existing provision with a single, clearly argued plan rather than a list of loose options.
634.tie_back: The kural names three abilities of a counsellor, examining a matter fully, choosing the course with care and stating a firm, clear conclusion, and the Beveridge Report is a model of all three.
634._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of thorough study leading to a decisive recommendation, though Beveridge was an appointed adviser rather than a minister.

635.event_title: Nizam al-Mulk founds the Nizamiyya colleges and writes the Book of Government
635.place: Baghdad and the Seljuq Empire (Iran and Iraq)
635.event: Nizam al-Mulk, a Persian from Tus, became vizier to the Seljuq sultan Alp Arslan in the 1060s and continued under his son Malik Shah, holding the office for about 30 years. He founded a network of colleges named Nizamiyyas after him, the most famous being the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, founded in 1067, where he appointed scholars such as al-Juwayni and al-Ghazali. He set down his views on government in the Siyasatnama, the Book of Government.
635.explanation: Nizam al-Mulk is remembered in Persian tradition as the model vizier, a statesman who was also a patron of learning and an author on the right conduct of rulers.
635.tie_back: The kural describes the ideal counsellor as one who knows what is right, is full of learning and always knows how things are to be done, and Nizam al-Mulk's long vizierate, colleges and treatise on government embody that combination.
635._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: he fits the learned, capable counsellor well, but his record is not spotless, so the kural's stress on moral knowledge is only partly shown.

636.event_title: Benjamin Franklin answers the House of Commons on the Stamp Act
636.place: House of Commons, London, United Kingdom
636.event: While the House of Commons, sitting as a Committee of the Whole, examined witnesses on colonial opposition to the Stamp Act, Benjamin Franklin was the principal witness on 13 February 1766. He answered 174 recorded questions, and by his own later notes 89 of them came from members of the Grenville ministry or other opponents. His answers were printed as The Examination of Doctor Benjamin Franklin, and the Stamp Act was repealed later in 1766.
636.explanation: Franklin's mix of quick wit and detailed knowledge of the colonies let him parry hostile questions and turn some of them to his own advantage, and the printed examination greatly raised his reputation.
636.tie_back: The kural asks what scheme can stand against a person who joins natural sharpness to learning, and Franklin's handling of dozens of hostile questions shows such a person proving hard to outwit.
636._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of sharp wit combined with deep knowledge defeating hostile questioning; the repeal itself had several causes besides Franklin's testimony.

637.place: Kongwa and other sites, Tanganyika (now Tanzania)
637.event: In 1947 Britain's Labour government launched a plan, run by the Overseas Food Corporation, to grow groundnuts on cleared land in Tanganyika to ease a post-war shortage of fats. It was commissioned after a survey completed in only seven weeks, with no pilot scheme, and it failed to allow for the area's soil and rainfall; at Kongwa there was enough rain for a groundnut crop only once between 1947 and 1951. The scheme was abandoned on 9 January 1951, with about 36.5 million pounds written off.
637.explanation: The planners relied on a plan drawn up on paper and on heavy machinery, while ignoring local conditions and the knowledge of local farmers, and the project collapsed.
637.tie_back: The kural warns that even someone who knows from books how a thing should be done must act only after learning how the world actually works, and the groundnut scheme failed for want of exactly that knowledge.
637._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural in negative form: an elaborate plan that ignored the real conditions of the land.

638.event_title: Hai Rui's memorial rebukes the Jiajing Emperor
638.event: The Ming Jiajing Emperor had for more than twenty years largely stopped holding court audiences and spent heavily on Daoist rituals and the search for longevity. In 1566 Hai Rui, a secretary in the Ministry of Revenue, submitted a memorial criticising the emperor for this neglect of government, and the emperor had him thrown into prison. Early in 1567, a few days after the emperor's death, Hai Rui was released and restored to his rank, and he was later honoured with the posthumous name Loyal and Incorruptible.
638.explanation: Hai Rui spoke plainly to a ruler who was known to punish critics, and his courage made him a lasting model of the honest official in China.
638.tie_back: The kural says that even when the ruler rejects wise advice and is ignorant himself, the one at his side must still tell him what is truly good, and Hai Rui did so at the cost of his freedom.
638._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: an official delivering unwelcome but beneficial counsel to a ruler who would not heed it.

639.event_title: The fall of Sejanus, Tiberius's trusted prefect
639.event: Sejanus, prefect of the Praetorian Guard, won the complete confidence of the emperor Tiberius and became the chief administrator of the empire, especially after Tiberius withdrew to Capri. He used his position to attack members of the imperial family who stood between him and power. In 31 CE, after Tiberius grew suspicious of his ambitions, a letter from the emperor was read in the Senate, Sejanus was arrested and condemned, and he was executed the same year.
639.explanation: The most dangerous threat to Tiberius came not from foreign enemies but from the minister he trusted most, who was suspected of plotting to take the throne.
639.tie_back: The kural says countless open enemies are better than one minister at one's side who plans one's ruin, and Sejanus is the classic Roman example of such a minister.
639._accuracy_note: A very close fit, with the caveat that the full extent of Sejanus's plot is debated by historians because the ancient sources are hostile to him.

640.event_title: Babbage's Difference Engine No. 1 is left unfinished
640.event: From 1821 Charles Babbage designed Difference Engine No. 1, the first complete design for an automatic calculating engine, and the British government paid for its construction. Only a demonstration section of about 2,000 parts, one-seventh of the whole, was completed in 1832; work halted after a dispute with his engineer Joseph Clement, and the government finally abandoned the project in 1842 after spending about 17,500 pounds. When the Science Museum later built his Difference Engine No. 2 from his drawings, completing the calculating section in 1991, the machine worked.
640.explanation: Babbage's designs were sound, as the modern reconstruction proved, but the project failed in the practical business of managing the engineer, the costs and the work through to completion.
640.tie_back: The kural says that those who lack the skill to carry things through leave their work unfinished even when they have planned it properly, and the brilliantly designed but never-completed Difference Engine is a striking case.
640._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of good design without completed execution, though funding and a dispute with the engineer, not only Babbage's own management, stopped the work.
